title: 27 Flood Deaths Unreported by Camp Mystic as Texas Camp Seeks Reopening - NewsBreak
text:
By Climate Cosmos Team ,
14 hours ago
The July 2025 Flood’s Devastating Toll (Image Credits: Unsplash)
Hunt, Texas — Texas lawmakers intensified scrutiny of Camp Mystic this week after the camp’s medical officer testified that she never reported 27 deaths from last summer’s catastrophic flood to state regulators, despite legal requirements. [1] [2] The revelation came amid legislative hearings probing the all-girls Christian summer camp’s operations, just as operators push to resume activities near the flood-ravaged site along the Guadalupe River. [3] Families of the victims and investigators have raised alarms over potential safety gaps that could endanger future campers.
The July 2025 Flood’s Devastating Toll Flash flooding struck central Texas on July 4, 2025, overwhelming communities in Kerr County and sending the Guadalupe River surging more than 30 feet in under two hours. [4] At Camp Mystic, a historic summer retreat hosting around 750 girls, the waters claimed 27 lives — 25 campers and two teenage counselors — in low-lying cabins such as Bubble Inn and Twins. [5] [6] The camp’s co-owner, Dick Eastland, also perished in the disaster, which contributed to over 130 fatalities across the region.
Rescue efforts stretched for days, with the camp initially reporting 27 confirmed deaths and several missing as of early July. [7] The tragedy unfolded before dawn, catching many in their sleep and highlighting the rapid onset of the floodwaters in the Texas Hill Country.
A Startling Oversight in Reporting During recent testimony before a Texas legislative committee, Camp Mystic’s chief medical officer acknowledged that the 27 flood-related deaths had not been formally reported to the state agency responsible for youth camps. [3] [8] State law mandates such notifications, yet nearly a year later, the records remained incomplete. Camp director Edward Eastland, son of the late co-owner, delivered a tearful apology to victims’ families during the same hearings. [9]
This admission has amplified concerns about transparency and accountability at the camp, which has faced lawsuits from grieving families alleging negligence in anticipating flood risks. [10] Lawmakers expressed dismay, questioning how such a fundamental step could have been overlooked amid ongoing investigations.
Investigators Highlight Preventable Failures A state investigative report presented to lawmakers detailed a series of lapses that rendered the deaths avoidable. [11] Camp leaders delayed evacuations despite warnings, failed to conduct door-to-door checks, and relied on untrained teenage counselors for emergency response. [4] All affected campers were within a short walk of higher-ground facilities, yet floodwaters overtook cabins by 3:26 a.m.
Lack of emergency training and drills for staff. Missing safety equipment and inadequate planning. No coordinated response to rising river levels. Overreliance on inexperienced teen counselors. [12] Investigator Casey Garrett outlined these shortcomings, emphasizing that timely action could have saved lives. [13] The findings have prompted calls for stricter oversight of summer camps in flood-prone areas.
What Matters Now Texas regulators have ordered Camp Mystic to revise its emergency plans before any license renewal. [14] A proposed Camp Safety Act, inspired by the tragedy, aims to enhance standards statewide.
Reopening Plans Meet Resistance Despite the controversies, Camp Mystic announced intentions to reopen for summer 2026, planning to welcome hundreds of new campers near the original site. [15] A judge recently blocked efforts to demolish flood-damaged cabins, preserving them potentially for legal proceedings. [16] Lawmakers grilled camp representatives on their fitness to operate, citing 27 cited deficiencies in safety protocols.
The hearings revealed deep divisions, with families sharing stories of loss while camp officials defended their improvements. [17] State officials must now weigh license renewal against these unresolved issues.
As Texas grapples with the legacy of the 2025 floods, the Camp Mystic case underscores the urgent need for robust safeguards in vulnerable recreational settings. Lawmakers’ deliberations could reshape camp regulations, ensuring that past failures do not foreshadow future risks. The path forward remains uncertain, but the stakes for young lives hang in the balance.
